# PREFACE.

It is now the ninth year since I boarded a ship in the company of the Most Illustrious Prince, the Duke of Albemarle <note>Christopher Monck, 2nd Duke of Albemarle (1653–1688)</note>, Supreme Governor of the Island of Jamaica, to serve as Physician to the same Prince. During the voyage, while staying on the islands of Madeira, Barbados, Nevis, Saint Christopher, and Jamaica, in my spare hours and those free from medical practice (which otherwise, by reason of my duty, was my primary concern), I observed natural things as much as I was able and as my poor health permitted. I committed these observations mostly to paper, though sometimes, due to the inconveniences of the location, I entrusted them to memory. In a short space of time in these new regions, situated at a great distance from our Europe, I found some plants, minerals, and animals to be exactly the same as those I had very often seen and handled in Europe. I also quickly discovered, from the many things noted by me and believed to be new, that in travel accounts—

<summary>The author introduces his voyage to Jamaica and the West Indies as the personal physician to the Duke of Albemarle, noting his methods for recording botanical and zoological observations.</summary>

# P R E F A C E

and that by the writers of Natural History <note>original: "Historiæ Naturalis"</note>, some things have been described excellently, others only somewhat well; while other things have long been recorded on account of this or that medicinal virtue, or this or that miraculous effect. I have likewise noticed that certain of these writers (to whom we nevertheless owe much) have compared and contrasted Indian and exotic natural objects with European ones with less accuracy and precision than is required. Thus, when dealing with vegetables <note>The author uses "Vegetabilibus" to refer to the broad category of plants and flora.</note>, for example, since they believed they retained the idea only of one or another commonly encountered European tree (namely, either the Walnut, the Fig, or the Pear), one traveler reported that a rare and new plant was similar to a Walnut <note>original: "Juglandi"</note>, another to a Fig <note>original: "ficui"</note>, or another to a Pear <note>original: "pyro"</note>. From this, the collectors and compilers of Natural History—who were accustomed to more accurate descriptions and had no other knowledge of these things except that which they had drawn from these men—took one and the same species found in various regions and described differently by different observers <note>original: "Observatoribus"</note>, and repeated or recorded it twice, three times, four times (indeed, authors of great name are found who have done so nine times). That is, they categorize, as they believe, nine plants differing in species;

<summary>The author critiques previous naturalists for inaccurately comparing exotic plants to common European trees, leading to the same species being mistakenly recorded as multiple distinct plants.</summary>
<keywords>natural history, botany, classification errors, exotic plants, European trees, scientific methodology, plant description</keywords>

# PREFACE

->...identity;<- <note>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing from the previous page regarding the identity of species.</note> although in reality it is one and the same plant named or recorded in regions located far apart from one another. For this reason, the **investigation of plants** <term>Plantarum investigatio: the systematic study and identification of flora</term> is abandoned by most as a difficult task, to the great detriment of medicine and the liberal arts. Therefore, being about to publish this small book, I deemed it necessary—lest I present plants already described as if they were new and undescribed—to collect their **synonyms** <note>original: "Synonyma"; here meaning the various names given to the same plant by different authors</note> from the accounts of voyagers and those recording natural history from the beginning. This was done so that the confusion which would otherwise necessarily arise might be removed, and so that the reader may see how much has been said among authors of this kind whom I happened to examine. 

In handing these down, if the description, the illustration, the title, or even just the name (from which the native localities of the herbs are known to us) of the author cited by me exactly matches the plant observed by me, I have no doubt that it is one and the same species of plant. If, however, it differs in a very few details, so that it is right to suspect such a difference, I consider such a variation to be rather a **variety** of the same plant, by reason of the climate, the soil, the cultivation, the age, the specimen, whether the stalk was well or poorly dried, or a defect or changed position of its parts, or finally, if my observations are less accurate, the matter thus...

# PREFACE

In such cases, these synonyms are followed by a question mark, so that the Reader may know I am doubtful whether this plant is one and the same as that observed by me, or rather a variety of the same, or a <term>sport of nature</term> <note>original: "naturæ lusus"; a term used by early naturalists to describe unusual biological variations or mutations that seemed to defy classification</note>. I would ask Authors who treat this kind of subject matter not to take such hesitation poorly, since I myself—although for the most part an eyewitness, equipped with specimens collected by my own hand in the places where they grow spontaneously, as well as with brief descriptions—remain uncertain about many of the plants reviewed in this little work as to whether they are distinct species. Nor do I doubt that many errors of every kind may be found in this little labor, brief though it is; for these, I hope the utility of the subject, its obscurity, and its confusion (but most especially my own insignificance and my inadequacy for untangling so many great difficulties) may obtain the Reader's pardon. The benevolent Reader will see that many conjectures presented here were not stated without cause or without merit when (God granting me life) he beholds the descriptions written in their native habitats, and the figures drawn to their natural size—some already engraved in copper, others yet to be engraved—as well as their virtues <note>The medicinal properties or "powers" of the plants</note> and

### Of the Island of Jamaica, etc.

A very tall, branched, hard or spurious sponge. <note>original: "Spongia dura seu spuria." In early modern botany, "spurious" or "false" was often used to describe organisms that shared the form of a group but had a different texture or substance.</note> Found together with the preceding species.

**Larger Spleenwort, with broader leaflets, lightly toothed, and eared on the upper side.** <note>original: "Lonchitis major, pinnis latioribus, leviter denticulatis, superiore latere auriculatis."</note> **Larger smooth Spleenwort.** <note>original: "Lonchitis glabra major."</note> Plumier, page 18, figure 27. It grows in the inland mountains of the Island of Jamaica.

**Smaller Spleenwort with broader leaflets, lightly toothed, eared on the upper side.** <note>original: "Lonchitis minor pinnis latioribus leviter denticulatis, superiore latere auriculatis."</note> It came out from the crevices of rocks on the banks of the river called **Rio d'oro** near **16 mile walk**. <note>A historic district in St. Catherine Parish, Jamaica, now known as Bog Walk.</note>

**Larger Spleenwort with narrower leaflets, lightly toothed, eared on the upper side.** <note>original: "Lonchitis major pinnis angustioribus leviter denticulatis superiore latere auriculatis."</note> I collected this growing with other plants of this kind in the shady and rocky inland forests.

**Larger Spleenwort with long and very narrow leaflets.** <note>original: "Lonchitis major pinnis longis angustissimisque."</note> I collected this growing in the crevices of rocks, on the shady road by which one goes to the place called **16 mile walk**.

**Smaller Polypody with sparse leaflets, ash-colored underneath.** <note>original: "Polypodium minus pinnulis raris subtus cinereis." Polypodium refers to the "many-footed" fern genus, named for its branching rhizomes.</note> **Fern-leaved or small Virginian fine-leaved polypody.** <note>original: "Filicifolia seu polypodium tenuifolium minus Virginianum."</note> Plukenet, table 89, figure 9. **Polypody with a thin and creeping root.** <note>original: "Polypodium radice tenui & repente."</note> Plumier, page 25, figure 36. It grows on rocks in the mountain forest near **Mr. Elletson's Plantation** in **Liguanee**. <note>Now the Liguanea plain, the site of modern-day Kingston.</note>

**Smaller Spleenwort with narrow, crowded, thin, dark green leaflets.** <note>original: "Lonchitis minor pinnulis angustis crebris tenuibus atrovirentibus."</note> **Thinner cut black Polypody.** <note>original: "Polypodium nigrum tenuius sectum."</note> Plumier, page 26, figure 37. [Found] with the prior plant.

**Anomalous tree related to Spleenwort with a winged leaf, bearing fruit from the notches of the leaflets.** <note>original: "Lonchitidi affinis arbor anomala folio alato e pinnarum crenis fructifero." The "fruit" refers to the sori or spore cases found on the edges of the leaves.</note> **American Phyllanthos, a plant producing flowers from each of the leaf-notches.** <note>original: "Phyllanthos Americana planta flores e singulis foliorum crenis proferens."</note> Paul Hermann, *Prodromus*, page 365. **American Epiphyllanthos related to Hemionitis, with a simply winged leaf, emulating the Horse-tongue plant, with a woody creeping root...** <note>original: "Hemionitidi affinis Americana epiphyllanthos, folio simpliciter pinnato, Hippoglossi æmulo, radice reptatrice lignosa..." This describes a plant that appears to grow flowers/fruit directly on its leaves.</note>

# Of the Island of Jamaica, etc.

...flowering at the notches of the leaves. <note>original: "ad foliorum crenas florida."</note> Plukenet, table 36, figure 7. It grows abundantly in the rocky, wooded hills near **Mr. Batchelour's house**.

**Larger Maidenhair with wavy leaflets, snow-white underneath.** <note>original: "Trichomanes majus pinnis sinuatis subtus niveis." At this time, "Trichomanes" was a broad term for various delicate ferns.</note> Among the rocks in a wooded hill, near **Mr. Elletson's Plantation** in **Liguanea**.

**Larger all-white Maidenhair with prickly leaflets of a trapezoid shape.** <note>original: "Trichomanes majus totum album pinnis aculeatis Trapezii figura."</note> This emerged from the crevices of drier rocks along the road where one travels the **16-mile walk**.

**Larger black Maidenhair with slightly toothed trapezoid leaflets.** <note>original: "Trichomanes majus nigrum pinnis leviter dentatis Trapezii figura."</note> It grew from rocky crevices on the banks of the **Rio d'Oro** <note>Spanish for "Golden River."</note>, and was also found in the rocky inland forests.

**Larger black Maidenhair with very wide and thin trapezoid leaflets.** <note>original: "Trichomanes majus nigrum, pinnas Trapezii figura latissimis tenuibus."</note> The gardener of **Sir Arthur Rawdon, Baronet**, brought this from the island of Jamaica; the most skilled botanist **Mr. Sherard** <note>William Sherard, a prominent patron of botany who helped compile these catalogs.</note> shared this plant with me.

**Maidenhair with longer leaflets, elegantly fringed, especially on the upper part.** <note>original: "Trichomanes foliolis longioribus eleganter superna præsertim parte laciniatis."</note> It emerged from rocky crevices on the banks of the **Rio d'Oro**, near **Mr. Philpot's Plantation** in the **16-mile walk**.

**Maidenhair with toothed leaflets, eared on the upper side.** <note>original: "Trichomanes, foliolis dentatis, superiore latere auriculatis." "Eared" or "auriculate" refers to the small, ear-like lobes at the base of the leaflets.</note> **Toothed rock-dwelling Spleenwort.** <note>original: "Polytrichum saxatile dentatum."</note> Plumier, page 35, figure 50 C. **Maritime Maidenhair with narrower segments.** <note>original: "Adiantum maritimum segmentis angustioribus."</note> Plukenet, *Phytographia*, table 124, figure 5. I found this on wet rocks by the banks of the **Rio d'Oro** toward the northern part of the island of Jamaica. The distinguished botanist **Mr. James Petiver** <note>A London apothecary and collector known for his massive museum of specimens.</note> showed me specimens of this sent to him from the islands of **Barbados and Bermuda**.

**Largest fern divided only into oblong and wide leaflets, not notched.** <note>original: "Filix maxima in pinnas tantum divisa oblongas latasque non crenatas."</note> I collected this growing on the sides of **Mount Diablo**.

**Large fern divided only into oblong and wide leaflets, not notched, gradually narrowing from a rounder base to the tip.** <note>original: "Filix major in pinnas tantum divisa oblongas latasque non crenatas à basi rotundiore ad apicem se sensim angustantes."</note> Is this the broad-leaved, non-branching fern, dusty with black spots <note>referring to the sori, or reproductive spores, on the underside</note>? Plumier, page 6, figure 9. This was brought from the island of Jamaica by the gardener of **Sir Arthur Rawdon, Baronet**, and **Mr. Sherard** shared it with me.

**Large climbing fern divided only into oblong and wide leaflets, not notched.** <note>original: "Filix major scandens in pinnas tantum divisa oblongas latasque non crenatas."</note> It climbs the larger tree trunks on the southern side of **Mount Diablo**, reaching a height of 20 or 30 feet. It is also found in the same place with notched leaves. Fern...

# Catalog of Plants

...**climbing, broad-leaved, and saw-toothed.** <note>original: "scandens latifolia serrata."</note> *Plumier, page 8, figure 12.* The *Panna-valli* <note>A local name for a climbing fern found in India, here being compared to Jamaican species.</note> in the *Hortus Malabaricus, part 12, page 69, plate 35.*

**Larger climbing Fern divided only into leaflets, which are oblong, very broad, and not notched.** <note>original: "Filix major scandens in pinnas tantum divisa..." "Notched" here refers to "crenated" or scalloped edges.</note> This was brought from the Island of **Jamaica** by the gardener of **Sir Arthur Rawdon, Baronet**, and shared with me by **Mr. Sherard**.

**Larger Fern divided only into leaflets, which are oblong, narrow, and not notched.** It grows abundantly on the banks of the **Rio d’Oro** <note>Spanish for "Golden River."</note> near **Archers Ridge**, between the **16-mile walk** and **St. Mary's**.

**Smaller Fern, mostly three-parted, with broad, oblong leaflets that are not notched.** <note>original: "Filix minor plerumque trifida..."</note> Could this be the *Indian Polypody with a Hart's-tongue appearance* <note>original: "Polypodium Indicum scolopendriæ facie"</note> according to **Breynius**, century 1, page 191? I collected this in the shady forests on the southern side of the mountain called **Diablo**.

**Larger three-parted eared Fern related to the Mule-fern, with very broad, wavy-edged leaflets.** <note>original: "Hemionitidi affinis Filix major Trifida auriculata..." "Auriculata" or "eared" refers to small lobes at the base of the leaflets.</note> Is this the *Caticaa* or *Polypody* of **Piso**, page 233? Or the *Greatest three-leaved Mule-fern* of **Plumier**, page 22, figure 21? I observed it growing on a shady and wooded hill near **the Orange-walk**, by the banks of the **Rio Cobre**, at the **Crescent Plantation**.

**Larger Fern divided only into leaflets, which are few, quite broad, oblong, striped, positioned opposite one another, and not notched.** <note>original: "Filix major in pinnas tantum divisa, raras..."</note> I collected this on the slopes of the inland mountain called **Diablo**.

**Larger Fern divided only into leaflets, which are few, oblong, broad, and notched.** <note>original: "Filix major in pinnas tantum divisa, raras, oblongas latasque crenatas."</note> This may be the *Fern or Polypody* of **Marcgrav**, page 2. Or the *Brazilian unbranched Fern with whole, saw-toothed leaves* described by **Breynius**, century 1, page 188. Or the *Broad-leaved unbranched Fern with rounded notches* of **Plumier**, page 7, figure 10. I observed it growing on the banks of the **Rio d’Oro** near the **16-mile walk**.

**Smaller Fern divided only into leaflets, which are numerous, mostly positioned opposite one another, oblong, broad, and notched.** It is found on **Mount Diablo**, at **Archers Ridge**, and in other inland forests of the Island of **Jamaica**.

**Smaller Fern divided only into leaflets, which are few, oblong, broad, and notched.** Found together with the previous species.

**Smaller Fern divided only into leaflets, which are numerous, not notched, eared at the lower side, and marked on the back with round, dusty spots.** <note>original: "pulverulentis areolis." These "dusty spots" are sori, the clusters of spores found on the underside of fern fronds.</note> It is found on the slopes of the mountain called **Diablo**.

**Smaller Fern divided only into leaflets, which are numerous, not notched, eared, and marked with dusty lines on the back.** <note>original: "lineis pulverulentis."</note> The *Lonchitis with dusty lines near the vein* <note>original: "Lonchitis juxta nervum pulverulenta."</note> of **Plumier**, page 20, figure 29. b. Found together with the previous species.

# Of the Island of Jamaica, etc.

**Small fern entirely covered in reddish down, divided only into leaflets, which are sparse, not notched, and somewhat round.** <note>original: "Filix minor ruffa lanugine tota obducta..." The "down" refers to the fuzzy or hairy texture common on certain fern fronds.</note> This very elegant plant was shared with me by **Mr. Sherard**, who received it from the gardener of **Sir Arthur Rawdon, Baronet**.

**Smaller fern, divided only into leaflets, positioned opposite each other, oblong and broad, not notched, with the lowest ones having ears at the base.** <note>original: "infimis ad basin auriculatis." In botany, "eared" or "auriculate" refers to small lobes at the base of the leaf that resemble earlobes.</note> It is found in the inland mountain forests of the **Island of Jamaica**.

***Branched three-parted Hart's-tongue fern.*** <note>original: "Phyllitis ramosa trifida."</note> Found in the inland forests of the **Island of Jamaica**.

***Climbing fern related to the many-parted Hart's-tongue,*** **divided only into leaflets, which are oblong, narrow, and not notched.** <note>original: "Phyllitidi multifidæ affinis filix scandens..."</note> Is this perhaps another species of fern from the **Island of Tamaraca** mentioned by **Marcgraf on page 2**? It climbs to a height of 12 or 15 feet on the tree trunks of **Mount Diablo**, **Archers Ridge**, and the **Mountain River Plantations**, as well as in other inland mountain forests of the **Island of Jamaica**.

***Climbing fern related to the many-parted Hart's-tongue,*** **divided only into leaflets, which are oblong, narrow, and jagged.** <note>original: "laciniatas" - meaning the edges are deeply and irregularly cut.</note> Is it a species of fern from **Marcgraf, page 2**? *The very beautiful Brazilian climbing fern* <note>original: "Filix scandens perpulchra Brasiliana."</note> by **Breynius, century 1, page 185**. *The anomalous exotic climbing fern* <note>original: "Filix scandens exotica anomala."</note> in **Ray’s History, page 153**. Could it be the *Isieru-valli-panna* or *Warapoli* in the **Hortus Malabaricus, part 12, page 65, plate 34**? Or the *Valli-panna* in **part 12, page 63, plate 32**? Or another *Isieru-valli-panna* in **part 12, page 67, plate 33**? <note>The *Hortus Malabaricus* was a massive 12-volume work on the plants of the Malabar coast of India; the author is comparing Jamaican ferns to these Indian specimens.</note> I observed it climbing the tree trunks in the forest near **Captain Heywood's Plantation** in **St. Mary's**, in the northern part of the **Island of Jamaica**.

**Very large unbranched fern, with sparse forks, and various leaflets—the lower ones being oblong and sharp, but the upper ones somewhat round like those of Spleenwort.** <note>original: "asplenij subrotundis." Asplenium is the genus for Spleenwort ferns.</note> It grows abundantly around the mountain called **Diablo**.

**Larger unbranched fern, with sparse forks and numerous broad, very small, and short prickly leaflets.** It occurs abundantly on the banks of the **Rio Cobre**, <note>Spanish for "Copper River."</note> along the road that goes from the town of **St. Jago de la Vega** <note>Now known as Spanish Town.</note> to the place called the **16-mile walk**.

**Larger unbranched fern, with sparse forks and very sparse long, narrow leaflets.** I collected this on the banks of the **Rio d’Oro** <note>Spanish for "Golden River."</note> between the **16-mile walk** and **St. Mary's**.

**Larger unbranched fern, with frequent forks and long, narrow leaflets.** ***The unbranched fern with wider teeth*** by **Plumier, page 11, figure 17**. Many varieties of this fern arose on the banks of the wooded inland rivers of this **Island of Jamaica**.

**Greater unbranched fern, with sparse and shorter branches, and thick, broad, short leaflets that are not prickly.** <note>original: "Filix non ramosa major, surculis raris brevioribus, pinnulis crebris latis brevibus non aculeatis."</note> **Dr. Sherard** <note>William Sherard (1659–1728) was a significant English botanist who contributed many specimens to Sloane.</note> shared this with me, having had it brought to him from the **Island of Jamaica**.

**Greater unbranched fern, with frequent branches and shorter, narrow leaflets.** <note>original: "Filix non ramosa major, surculis crebris, pinnulis brevioribus angustis."</note> Is this perhaps the ***second species of exotic fern, or the Brazilian unbranched fern with sharper spleenwort-like leaves*** mentioned by Breynius in *Centuria 1, page 187*? It is found on the rocky banks of the rivers called **Orange River** and **Rio d'Oro**, between **Sixteen Mile Walk** and **St. Mary’s**.

**Smaller unbranched fern, with frequent branches and long, broad leaflets.** Found with the former.

**Smaller unbranched fern, with frequent branches and very short, narrow leaflets.** I collected this below the town of **St. Jago de la Vega** <note>The former Spanish capital of Jamaica, now known as Spanish Town.</note> along the banks of the river called the **Cobre**.

**Smallest unbranched fern, with frequent branches and very short, narrow leaflets.** Found with the former.

**Very small unbranched fern, with frequent branches and very narrow, sparse leaflets.** Found by shady inland streams.

**Unbranched climbing fern, with broad, long, frequent leaflets that are blunt and notched.** <note>original: "Filix non ramosa scandens, pinnulis latis, longis, crebris, obtusis & dentatis."</note> Known as ***Para-panna-Maravaca*** in the *Hortus Malabaricus*, part 11, page 31, plate 15. It was found winding around the larger trees on the sides of the inland mountains called **Mount Diablo** and **Archers Ridge**.

**Smaller unbranched fern with a black stalk, sparse branches, and narrow, notched, sparse, short, sharp leaflets that are snowy-white underneath.** <note>This is likely the Silver Fern (Pityrogramma calomelanos), known for the white waxy powder on the underside of its fronds.</note> Known as the ***American black Maidenhair sprinkled with very white powder*** by Breynius; the ***American Calomelanos Maidenhair, or black Maidenhair with leaves very white on the underside*** by Plukenet; the ***Fern similar to black Maidenhair sprinkled with very white powder*** by Plumier; the ***Smaller Maidenhair*** by Marcgrave; and the ***Conambai miri*** or a species of Maidenhair by Piso. It is found on shady inland rocks on the islands of **Jamaica** and **Barbados**.

**Smallest unbranched fern with a black stalk, sparse branches, and narrow, sparse, short, sharp leaflets that are snowy-white underneath.** Found with the former.

**Greater unbranched fern with a black stalk, sparse branches, and narrow, sparse, long, notched leaflets.** Found on the rocks by the banks of the **Orange River** and **Rio d'Oro** near **Mr. Philpott’s Plantation** in the northern part of the **Island of Jamaica**.

**Smaller unbranched fern, with a black stalk, sparse shoots, and broad, toothed leaflets that are white underneath.** <note>original: "Filix non ramosa minor, caule nigro, furculis raris, pinnulis latis dentatis subtus niveis."</note> I found this on the **Islands of Barbados** or **Nevis**.

**Very small unbranched fern, resembling Wall-rue, with nearly round, deeply split leaflets.** <note>original: "Rutæ murariæ accedens Filicula non ramosa minima, pinnulis subrotundis profunde scissis." Wall-rue (*Asplenium ruta-muraria*) is a small fern often found in wall crevices.</note> This grew out of the crevices of rocks along the banks of the **Rio d'Oro** <note>The "Golden River," a tributary of the Rio Cobre.</note> between **Sixteen Mile Walk** and **St. Mary's**.

**Small unbranched fern, resembling Wall-rue, with nearly round, deeply split leaflets.** <note>original: "Rutæ murariæ accedens Filix minor non ramosa, pinnulis subrotundis profunde scissis."</note> This is the ***Fern with crested leaflets*** described by **Plumier** <note>Charles Plumier (1646–1704), a French botanist who extensively documented Caribbean flora.</note> on page 16, figure 25. A. Found with the previous variety.

**Greater Wall-rue with various leaves, specifically: oblong and whole, or nearly round and serrated.** <note>original: "Ruta muraria major foliis variis, scil. oblongis integris & subrotundis serratis."</note> It grew from the fissures of rocks on the banks of the **Orange River** and **Rio d'Oro** on the **Island of Jamaica**.

**Greatest Wall-rue with oblong, notched leaves.** <note>original: "Ruta muraria maxima foliis oblongis crenatis."</note> Found with the previous variety.

**Smaller unbranched fern, with frequent, blunt, and notched leaflets.** <note>original: "Filix non ramosa minor, pinnulis crebris, obtusis, crenatis."</note> Found with the preceding varieties.

**Greatest black unbranched maidenhair fern, with frequent, larger, thick leaflets shaped like a trapezoid.** <note>original: "Adiantum nigrum maximum non ramosum pinnis crebris, majoribus crassis & Trapezii in modum figuratis." *Adiantum* is the genus for Maidenhair ferns, known for their delicate, water-repellent foliage.</note> This is called ***Avenca*** by an anonymous Portuguese author in **Purchas** <note>Samuel Purchas, an English compiler of travel narratives.</note> book 7, chapter 1, page 1312. It is also the ***Conambai-miri*** or the first species of Maidenhair, or ***Avenca*** to the Portuguese, described by **Piso** <note>Willem Piso (1611–1678), a Dutch physician and naturalist who wrote about the natural history of Brazil.</note> on page 234. It is found frequently on the banks of the torrent beyond the **Troopers' Quarters** near the town of **St. Jago de la Vega** <note>Now known as Spanish Town.</note> and in the inland forests of the **Island of Jamaica**.

**Greater black unbranched maidenhair fern, with rarer, thick leaflets shaped like a trapezoid.** <note>original: "Adiantum nigrum majus non ramosum, pinnulis & furculis rarioribus, crassis & Trapezii in modum figuratis."</note>

**Branched black maidenhair fern, powdery and sickle-shaped.** <note>original: "Adiantum nigrum ramosum pulverulentum & falcatum."</note> Mentioned by **Plumier**, page 32, figure 47. Found everywhere in the inland forests.

**Smaller black unbranched maidenhair fern, with larger, thick leaflets shaped like a trapezoid.** <note>original: "Adiantum nigrum minus non ramosum, pinnulis majoribus crassis Trapezii in modum figuratis."</note> This is the ***Eared, branched Barbados maidenhair with very minutely toothed, thicker segments*** mentioned by **Plukenet** <note>Leonard Plukenet (1642–1706), a British botanist and gardener to Queen Mary II.</note> in his *Phytographia*, table 125, figure 2. Found along the paths on the mountain called **Archer’s Ridge** and in other inland forests of the **Island of Jamaica**.

**Greater black unbranched maidenhair fern, with larger, thin leaflets shaped like a trapezoid.** <note>original: "Adiantum nigrum non ramosum, majus pinnulis majoribus tenuibus Trapezii in modum figuratis."</note> Found with the previous variety.

**Greater black unbranched maidenhair fern, with sparse shoots and dense, thick, very small crested leaflets shaped like a trapezoid.** <note>original: "Adiantum nigrum non ramosum majus, furculis raris pinnulis densis crassis minimis cristatis & Trapezii in modum figuratis."</note> This is the ***First species of exotic fern, or the Brazilian unbranched fern with crested leaflets*** described by **Breynius** <note>Jacob Breyne (1637–1697), a Polish businessman and botanist.</note> in *Centuria 1*, page 187. Also the ***Branched maidenhair with toothed trapezoid leaves*** by **Plumier**, page 31, figure 46. Found in the mountain forests near **Mr. Elletson's Plantation** in **Liguanea** <note>The Liguanea plain is the site of modern-day Kingston and St. Andrew.</note>, **Archer’s Ridge**, etc.

# Catalogue of Plants

**Greater unbranched black maidenhair, with shoots proceeding from the top of a common stalk as if from a center, and radiating in the manner of a star.** <note>original: "Adiantum nigrum majus non ramosum, surculis è pediculi communis summitate tanquam centro prodeuntibus & stellæ in modum radiatis."</note> *The Maidenhair of Du Tertre*, <note>original French: "Polytric du Tertre," p. 88. Jean-Baptiste du Tertre was a French Dominican missionary and botanist.</note> page 88. *Radiated branched maidenhair*, <note>original Latin: "Adiantum ramosum radiatum," Plum. p. 33. fig. 49.</note> Plumier, page 33, figure 49. In the woods not far from **Captain Drax’s Plantation**, and near the city once called **Seville** <note>The early Spanish capital, Sevilla la Nueva, in northern Jamaica.</note> in the northern part of the Island of Jamaica.

**Branched, thorny tree fern with an undivided trunk, and broad, dense, short, thin, minutely toothed leaflets.** <note>original: "Filix arborea ramosa spinosa caudice non diviso, pinnulis latis densis brevibus tenuibus minutim dentatis."</note> Perhaps the *Ferns thicker than a spear* <note>original Latin: "An Filices hasta crassiores," Petr. Martyr. decad?</note> of Peter Martyr's *Decades*? *Fern trees of these parts and the island of Hispaniola* <note>original Spanish: "Arboles del Helecho d’estas partes y ysla Española," Oviedo Coronica. lib. 9. cap. 14?</note> from Oviedo's *Chronicle*, book 9, chapter 14? *A sort of fern altogether admirable* <note>original French: "Sorte de Fougere tout a fait admirable," du Tertre. p. 89?</note> of Du Tertre, page 89? It grows most copiously on the mountain called **Diablo** <note>Mount Diablo, a prominent peak in Jamaica.</note> and on the banks of torrents in the mountainous places between **Guanaboa** and **St. Faiths**.

**Branched tree fern, with an undivided trunk, and narrow, sparse, blunt, whole leaflets.** <note>original: "Filix arborea ramosa, caudice non diviso, pinnulis angustis raris obtusis integris."</note> I collected this wonderful species of fern toward the summit of the mountain which makes up the largest part of the Island of **Nevis** <note>original: "Nieves."</note>, on the banks of a steep torrent where it was growing copiously.

**Very large branched black maidenhair, with blunt leaflets or pinnae, variously but most beautifully lobed and toothed.** <note>original: "Adiantum nigrum ramosum maximum, foliis seu pinnulis obtusis varie sed pulcherrime sinuatis & dentatis."</note> *Branched and berry-bearing black maidenhair*, <note>original Latin: "Adiantum nigrum ramosum & bacciferum," Plum. p. 31. fig. 45.</note> Plumier, page 31, figure 45. Copiously and everywhere on the sides of the mountain called **Diablo**.

**Very large branched black maidenhair, with thin blunt leaflets or pinnae, regularly, very minutely and beautifully cut.** <note>original: "Adiantum nigrum ramosum maximum, foliis seu pinnulis obtusis tenuibus, regulariter minutissime & pulcherrime sectis."</note> Perhaps the *Exotic fern with very long and narrow toothed branches* <note>original Latin: "An filix exotica prælongis & angustis ramulis denticulata," Pluck. phyt. tab. 181. fig. 3?</note> of Plukenet's *Phytographia*, plate 181, figure 3? Found with the previous variety and at the banks of the **Rio d'Oro** and **Orange River** toward **St. Mary’s** in the northern part of **Jamaica**.

**Branched climbing maidenhair, with oblong, deeply slashed, transparent pinnae or leaflets.** <note>original: "Adiantum ramosum scandens, pinnulis seu foliis oblongis profundè laciniatis pellucidis."</note> It climbs the larger trunks of trees in the inland mountains called **Diablo** and **Archers Ridge**. Mr. **George Handyfyd** brought the same from Tierra del Fuego in the Strait of Magellan and gave it to me as a gift.

**Greater branched maidenhair, with long, thin, deeply slashed, blunt leaflets or pinnae.** <note>original: "Adiantum ramosum majus, foliis seu pinnulis tenuibus longis profundè laciniatis obtusis."</note> I collected this on the Island of **Madeira** beyond the city of **Funchal**, on the road where one goes up the mountain.

**Very large branched black maidenhair, with long, thin, sharp, thorny leaflets or pinnae.** <note>original: "Adiantum nigrum ramosum maximum, foliis seu pinnulis tenuibus longis acutis spinosis."</note> It grows most copiously on **Mount Diablo**.

# The Island of Jamaica, etc.

**Greater branched black maidenhair, with thin, long, sharp, and thorny leaves or leaflets.** <note>original: "Adiantum nigrum ramosum majus, foliis seu pinnulis tenuibus longis acutis spinosis."</note> Found with the former.

**Smaller branched black maidenhair, with smaller, thin, blunt, and notched leaflets.** <note>original: "Adiantum nigrum ramosum minus, pinnulis minoribus tenuibus obtusis crenatis."</note> Found with the preceding ones.

**Smaller branched black maidenhair, with sparse, very small, and somewhat round branches, shoots, and leaflets.** It is found among the rocks below the city called **St. Jago de la Vega** <note>Now known as Spanish Town, the former capital of Jamaica.</note> near the river on this side.

**Maidenhair, or Venus-hair fern.** <note>original: "Adiantum sive capillus Veneris."</note> Cited by Jean Bauhin and in John Ray’s *History of Plants*, page 147. Master **Sherard** <note>William Sherard (1659–1728), a prominent English botanist who helped fund many scientific expeditions.</note> shared this, having had it brought to him from the Island of Jamaica.

**Greater branched black maidenhair with a coriander leaf.** <note>original: "Adiantum nigrum majus ramosum coriandri folio."</note> **Shrubby Bermuda maidenhair** with the highest branches upright and tapering into a conical shape. <note>original: "Adiantum fruticosum Bermudense summis ramulis erectis & in metæ formam fastigiatis."</note> Plukenet, plate 124, figure 1. I observed this on the banks of a shady, wooded stream beyond **Troopers Quarters** near the city of **St. Jago de la Vega**, and in other forests of the Island of **Jamaica**. Master **James Petiver** <note>A London apothecary and fellow of the Royal Society known for his massive natural history collections.</note> showed it to me, having had it brought from the Island of Bermuda.

**Largest branched black maidenhair, with larger leaves shaped like a trapezium.** <note>A four-sided shape with at least one pair of parallel sides.</note> I observed this most beautiful species of maidenhair growing in the larger inland forests.

**Largest branched climbing fern, with sparse branches and crowded, broad, short, and blunt leaflets.** I observed this fern climbing trees everywhere in the inland forests on the road where one goes from **Guanaboa** <note>Guanaboa Vale in St. Catherine parish.</note> toward **Colonel Bourden’s Plantation**, and on the sides of **Mount Diablo** and **Archers Ridge**.

**Greater branched fern with a thorny stalk, and round leaflets that are deeply jagged, or like the leaves of chervil.** <note>original: "Filix ramosa major caule spinoso, foliis seu pinnulis rotundis profunde laciniatis, seu cerefolii foliis." Chervil is a delicate herb related to parsley.</note> I collected this growing in the fields near **Rio d’Oro** <note>The "Golden River" in Jamaica.</note> not far from **Mr. Philpott’s Plantation**.

**Greater branched fern, with crowded, short, broad, blunt, and somewhat round leaflets.** Is it the *Tancapaz* of **Hernandez**? <note>Francisco Hernández de Toledo, a physician who documented Mexican plants in the 16th century.</note> Found everywhere in the inland forests of the Island of Jamaica.

**Greater branched fern, with long, sharp, sparse, and sickle-shaped leaflets.** <note>original: "Filix ramosa major, pinnulis longis, acutis, raris, falcatis."</note> **Fern with the blunt leaflets of a Holly-fern**, not toothed, and dusty at the edges. <note>original: "Filix pinnulis lonchitidis obtusis, non dentatis ad oras pulverulentis." The "dust" refers to the spores (sori) on the underside of the fern.</note> Plumier, page 10, figure 14. Is it the **Brazilian fern** of Marcgrave, page 2? Or the *Conambaia* or fern of Piso, page 233? <note>Willem Piso and Georg Marcgrave co-authored the *Historia Naturalis Brasiliae* (1648).</note> I collected this in the inland parts of the Island of Jamaica.

**Greater hairy branched fern, with sparse branches and leaflets like Spleenwort**—namely, crowded, broad, short, somewhat round, and not toothed. <note>original: "Filix ramosa major hirsuta, ramulis raris, pinnulis asplenii, scil. crebris, latis brevibus subrotundis non dentatis."</note>

# Catalog of Plants

### Page 30

**Grass with a single spike like quaking-grass, with larger spikelets that are hairy and purplish.** <note>original: "Gramen spica brizæ singulari..." Briza is a genus of grasses known as quaking-grass due to their fluttering spikelets.</note> It is found in the meadows around the place called *Seven Plantations*.

**The largest panic-grass with a divided spike, armed with awns.** <note>An 'awn' is a hair- or bristle-like appendage found on the husks of many grasses.</note> **Caspar Bauhin**, *Pinax*, page 8: "The second panic-grass with a spike armed with long awns." <note>original: "Gramen paniceum secundum..."</note> By the same author, *Theatri Botanici*, page 137: "Panic-grass, or wild panic, armed with awns." **Lobelius**, *Icones*, page 14: "A grass with the appearance of panic-grass, surrounded by awns." **Tabernaemontanus**, page 557: "The second panic-grass." **Gerard**, revised edition, page 16: "The second panic-grass." **Parkinson**, page 1155: "Wild panic with long awns." **Jean Bauhin**, volume 2, book 17, page 443: "A type of grass called by some Frenchmen 'the second dog’s-tooth' or 'wild panic with a scattered panicle'." <note>original: "dens caninus secundus..."</note> **Chabraeus**, page 179. I have heard that it grows naturally in marshy places around the locations called *Wague water* and *Agua alta* <note>Spanish for "Deep Water."</note> in Jamaica, and in that part of the island of Barbados called *Scotland*. The stalks <note>original: "culmi"</note> of this grass are planted in great abundance in wetter lands in the manner of sugar canes; there, they sprout profusely at the joints <note>original: "internodia"</note> and provide fodder <note>original: "pabulum"</note> for horses, cattle, etc.

**Larger panic-grass with a simple smooth spike, with grains sitting on small stalks.** I found this in the place called *Guanaboa* along with the preceding one.

**Panic-grass with a simple smooth spike.** **Ray**, *Historia Plantarum*, page 1261. It grows copiously in the meadows between *Black River Bridge* and the town of *St. Jago de la Vega*. <note>Now known as Spanish Town, Jamaica.</note>

**Smallest panic-grass spread upon the ground, with a divided awnless spike and variegated leaves.** Is it perhaps the Ceylonese grass with elegantly spotted leaves mentioned in **Hermann**, *Paradisus Batavus Prodromus*, page 338? Or the smaller panic-grass with a scattered spike from the island of Barbados in **Plukenet**, *Phytographia*, table 189, figure 5? It grows on the borders of paths and in meadows around the town of *St. Jago de la Vega*.

<margin>**Cenchrus echinatus** <note>Now commonly known as Southern Sandbur.</note></margin>
**The largest prickly grass with a red or white spike.** **Commelin**, *Catalog of the Plants of Curaçao*, page 338: "Prickly grass of Curaçao." **Schola Botanica**, page 258: "American grass with a prickly spike and larger spikelets." **Plukenet**, table 92, figure 3. Is it perhaps the same as the "Jointed grass with short leaves resembling prickles from Madras" by the same author, table 189, figure 3? After rains, it grows copiously and everywhere in the fields of the Caribbean islands and Jamaica.

<margin>**Cenchrus tribuloides** <note>Commonly known as Sanddune Sandbur.</note></margin>
**Creeping maritime prickly grass with a longer stalk and leaner spikes.** I collected this on the small sandy island called *Gun cayos* <note>Gun Cay, a small island off the coast of Port Royal.</note> not far from the city of *Port-Royal*.

**Tall slender reed** <note>original Latin: "Arudo alta gracilis"</note>, with greenish-blue leaves and smaller spikelets <note>original Latin: "locustis minoribus"; in botanical Latin of this period, "locusta" referred to the spikelet of a grass</note>. Is it perhaps the *Carrizos* <note>Spanish for "reeds"</note> mentioned by **Oviedo** <note>Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo y Valdés, a 16th-century Spanish historian and naturalist</note> in book 10, chapter 6? **The Trumpet Reed.** It grows abundantly on the banks of the lagoon not far from **Passage Fort** <note>An important early English fortification and port in Jamaica, located near present-day Portmore</note>.

**Large two-horned woolly finger-grass** <note>original Latin: "Gramen dactylon bicorne tomentosum maximum"</note>, with very numerous spikes. The tenth species of grass, called **Capûpuba** by the Brazilians; the "plumed grass" of **Marcgrave** <note>Georg Marcgrave, a German naturalist who co-authored a major work on the natural history of Brazil (1648)</note>, page 2. **Capijpuba** in **Piso** (1648 edition), page 102. **Capuupeba** in the same (1658 edition), page 238. This most beautiful species of grass occurs abundantly on the Island of **Nevis** and in **Jamaica** near the place called **The Angels** <note>An early settlement area in St. Catherine Parish, Jamaica</note>, etc.

**Smaller two-horned woolly finger-grass** <note>original Latin: "Gramen dactylon bicorne tomentosum minus"</note>. It grows abundantly in the meadows called **Palmetto Savanna** and **Limetree Savanna** toward the **Seven Plantations**. It is also found occasionally in the meadows around **Mr. Batchelour's Plantation** toward **Black River Bridge**.

**Finger-grass with short, thick spikes** <note>original Latin: "Gramen dactylon spicis brevibus crassis"</note>, usually four in number and arranged in the shape of a cross. **Egyptian finger-grass** of **Caspar Bauhin** <note>C. B. pin., a standard botanical reference of the era</note>, page 7; his *Theatrum Botanicum*, page 110. **Parkinson**, page 1179. **Grass of the cross** <note>original Arabic: "Nejem elm salib"</note> in **Alpini** <note>Prospero Alpini, an Italian physician and botanist who studied Egyptian plants</note>. **Cross grass** or **Grass of the cross** in **Jean Bauhin**, volume 2, book 17, page 460. **Cross grass** or **Grass of the cross of the Egyptians** according to **Alpini**; **Chabrey**, page 180. **Cruciate grass** in **Bontius**, page 148. **Cavara-pullu** in the *Hortus Malabaricus* <note>H. M.; a monumental 12nd-volume work on the plants of the Malabar Coast of India</note>, part 12, page 131. Is it perhaps the **Egyptian Star Grass** of **Vesling**? It flourishes everywhere by paths and in meadows.

**Taller finger-grass with many woolly spikes**. Perhaps the first species of grass in **Marcgrave**, page 1? Perhaps **Kouda-pullu** from the *Hortus Malabaricus*, part 12, page 95, plate 51? It abounds everywhere in the meadows around **Two Mile Wood**, etc.

**Thick and greener prostrate finger-grass** <note>original Latin: "Gramen dactylon procumbens crassum & viridius"</note> with a reclining stalk. The **American cruciate finger-grass**, called **Dutch Grass** by our countrymen in **Barbados**. **Plukenet**, *Phytographia*, plate 189, figure 7. Is it perhaps the more beautiful **Bermuda blood-grass** <note>original Latin: "Gramen Ischæmon Bermudense"</note> with short, blunt leaves in the same work, plate 245, figure 1? **Dutch Grass.** It occurs abundantly in the meadows of the islands of **Jamaica** and **Barbados** along the paths.

**Finger-grass with more slender spikes**, usually four in number and arranged in the shape of a cross. This species of grass is very common and met with everywhere in the meadows.

**Creeping two-horned finger-grass** <note>original Latin: "Gramen dactylon bicorne repens"</note> with short, broad leaves. **Tereta-pullu** in the *Hortus Malabaricus*, part 12, page 81, plate 44. In the wetter meadows and pastures of the **Caribbean Islands** and **Jamaica**.

### *Herbs with a less perfect or apetalous flower.* <note>The term "apetalous" refers to plants whose flowers lack petals, which early botanists categorized as "imperfect."</note>

**Tree-like stinging nettle with narrow, oblong leaves.** <note>original: *Urtica urens arborea foliis oblongis angustis.*</note> I collected this growing among the trees in the woods near *the Angels* <note>A settlement on the road between Spanish Town and the interior.</note> beyond the *Rio Cobre* river.

**Shrubby clustered nettle, narrow-leaved with a three-seeded fruit.** <note>original: *Urtica racemosa fruticosa angustifolia fructu tricocco.*</note> Is this perhaps the *Pino* of the Brazilians described by Marcgrave on page 48? Or the *Pino* or nettle described by Piso on page 233? I found this plant on one of the Caribbean Islands.

**Climbing clustered nettle, narrow-leaved with a three-seeded fruit.** <note>original: *Urtica racemosa scandens angustifolia fructu tricocco.*</note> Is this perhaps the *Valli-schoriganam* mentioned in the *Hortus Malabaricus*, part 2, page 79? <note>The *Hortus Malabaricus* was a monumental 17th-century treatise on the flora of the Malabar Coast of India; the author is comparing Jamaican species to those found in Asia.</note> It grows abundantly in the thickets of the meadows around the city of *St. Jago de la Vega* <note>Now known as Spanish Town.</note> and elsewhere.

**Lower, harmless clustered nettle.** <note>original: *Urtica racemosa humilior iners.* The term "iners" (inert) indicates that this species does not possess the stinging hairs typical of most nettles.</note> I discovered this on the banks of the river called *Cobre* near *Mr. Fonseca's Plantation*.

**Nettle with a woody stem and thinner, dark green leaves.** <note>original: *Urtica, caule lignoso, foliis tenuioribus atrovirentibus.*</note> Is this perhaps the branched Portuguese stinging nettle described in Commelin's Amsterdam Catalog, page 369? I collected this on the Island of *Madeira* near the city of *Funchal*.

**Harmless clustered woodland nettle with a veined leaf.** <note>original: *Urtica iners racemosa sylvatica, folio nervoso.*</note> I observed this occurring in the shady woods near the *Hope River* in *Liguanea* <note>The area of modern-day Kingston.</note> and in the shady, wooded mountains not far from *Colonel Cope's Plantation* in *Guanaboa*.

**Smaller harmless spiked nettle with a rounded, saw-toothed leaf and a three-seeded fruit.** <note>original: *Urtica minor iners spicata, folio subrotundo serrato, fructu tricocco.*</note> This arises everywhere in the sandy places of the meadows around the city of *St. Jago de la Vega*, especially toward the place called *2 mile wood*.

**Greater clustered lower nettle, prickly but not stinging.** <note>original: *Urtica major racemosa humilior, pungens sed non urens.* This distinction is important: the plant has sharp hairs that may prick the skin ("pungens") but lacks the chemical irritant that causes a burning sensation ("urens").</note> I collected this growing on the banks of the river called *Cobre* on the opposite side above the city of *St. Jago de la Vega*.

**Taller Ragweed with dark green, rough, and scented mugwort-leaves, not woolly.** <note>original: *Ambrosia elatior foliis artemisiæ atrovirentibus asperis odoratis, non lanuginosis.*</note> This is the *Katu-Tsietti pu* of the *Hortus Malabaricus*, part 10, page 89, plate 45; otherwise called the Malabar Ragweed with a very fragrant mugwort leaf and yellow flowers by Commelin in the same work. Is it perhaps the *Ytzequinpatli* described by Hernández on page 446? I observed it growing among stones near the river called *Dry River*, as well as in other inland places of the Island of Jamaica.

**American Castor Oil plant with clustered, bristly fruit.** <note>original: *Ricinus Americanus fructu racemoso hispido.* Known today as *Ricinus communis*.</note> Described by Jonston in *Dendrographia*, page 217. It is the *Nhambu Guacu* or *Figuero d’Inferno* <note>original Portuguese: "Fig-tree of Hell," a common name for the castor plant due to the purgative and toxic nature of its seeds.</note> of Piso (1648 edition).

# The Island of Jamaica, etc.

**Sicilian spiked Amaranth with a perennial root.** <note>original: "Amarantus siculus spicatus radice perenni." Amaranthus is a genus of herbs known for their dense flower clusters.</note> *Boccone; Ray’s History of Plants, p. 203.* It is found in ditches around the city of **Spanish Town** <note>original: "St. Jago de la Vega," the historic capital of Jamaica.</note>.

**Amaranth with a yellowish, slender, and silky panicle.** <note>original: "Amarantus panicula flavicante gracili holosericea"</note> It is found in hedges at the place called **Guanahoa** and in the **Caribbean Islands**.

**Greater climbing white Blite.** <note>original: "Blitum album majus scandens." "Blite" is a historical term for plants related to spinach and amaranth.</note> Is it perhaps the **Upright large-seeded Barbados Blite** <note>original: "Blitum Barbadense erectum megasporon"</note> of Plukenet’s *Phytographia*, table 151, figure 3? **Common smaller upright Blite.** <note>original: "Blitum vulgare minus surrectum"</note> *Munting’s Cultivated Plants, p. 291.* Perhaps the **smaller creeping variety** of the same author? **Smaller white many-seeded Blite with a roundish leaf.** <note>original: "Blitum minus album polyspermon folio subrotundo"</note> Called **Cararu** by the Brazilians and **Bredos** by the Portuguese. *Marcgrave, p. 13.* **Cararu, a species of American Blite**, *Piso, p. 241.* **Brazilian Blite called Cararu by Brazilians and Bredos by the Portuguese**, *Ray’s History of Plants, p. 201.* Is it the **Bletti** mentioned by Ferdinand Columbus, p. 57? Or the **Nexhoautli** of Hernandez, p. 269? Or Ximenez? **Culilu**, or **Caterpillars**. <note>A local common name likely referring to the shape of the flower spikes.</note> It flourishes luxuriously and abundantly everywhere in open fields after the rains.

**Knotweed-like Blite, green or variegated with green and white, many-flowered.** <note>original: "Blitum polygonoides viride seu ex viridi & albo variegatum polyanthos"</note> It is found here and there in waste places and muddy spots around the city of **Spanish Town**.

# Catalog of Plants

**The third species of wild Orach.** <note>original: "Atriplex sylvestris 3^a." Orach is a herb related to spinach, often used as a potherb.</note> *Morison, p. 604; Matthiolus, p. 362; Lugdunensis, p. 536.* **Goosefoot**, *by the same author, p. 542; Fuchs, p. 655; Lonicer, folio 101; Dodoens, p. 616; Camerarius’s Garden, p. 122; Frankfurt Botanical, p. 190.* **The fourth species of Nightshade**, *Tragus, p. 304.* **The fourth species of Blite**, *by the same author, p. 714.* **Wild Orach or Broad-leaved Goosefoot with jagged segments**, *Adversaria, p. 97; Lobel’s Images, p. 254.* **Broad-leaved wild Orach Goosefoot, the third Orach**, *Matthiolus in Lobel’s Observations, p. 128.* **Another kind of Dog’s Mercury**, <note>original: "Cynocrambe alterum genus."</note> *Caesalpino, p. 161.* **The first species of Goosefoot**, <note>original: "Chenopodium 1^um."</note> *Tabernaemontanus, p. 142.* **The second species of wild Orach**, *Schwenckfeld, p. 26.* **Broad-leaved wild Orach or Goosefoot**, *Gerard emended, p. 328; Parkinson, p. 749; Ambrosini’s Garden, p. 12.* **The Orach called Goosefoot**, *Johann Bauhin, vol. 2, book 23, p. 975; Chabrey, p. 306.* **The Blite called Orach, wild and broad-leaved**, *Commelin’s Amsterdam Catalog.* *Goosefoot*, or *Sowbane*. I collected this growing along the roadsides around the city of **Spanish Town** <note>original: "St. Jago de la Vega."</note>.

**Pellitory with leaves growing opposite each other and a cluster-bearing nettle flower.** <note>original: "Parietaria foliis ex adverso nascentibus, urticæ racemiferæ flore." Pellitory-of-the-wall was traditionally used for medicinal purposes.</note> It is frequently seen on shady and moist rocks.

**Shrubby, cone-bearing Glasswort with a white flower.** <note>original: "Kali fruticosum coniferum flore albo." Kali or Glasswort is a salt-tolerant plant formerly burned to produce soda ash for glassmaking.</note> *Another sort of Sampier* <note>original: "Sampier," an older spelling of Samphire.</note>. It is found everywhere in sandy maritime marshes near the place called **Passage-Fort**.

**Clear Water-Rupturewort.** <note>original: "Herniaria lucida aquatica." Rupturewort was historically believed to treat hernias.</note> It is common on riverbanks and in the crevices of moist rocks.

**A plant related to the Jute-mallow, with a Germander leaf, a stamen-like flower, and black quadrangular seeds arranged in a double row.** <note>original: "Corchoro affinis, chamædryos folio..." Corchorus is the genus that provides jute fiber.</note> It grows frequently in stony places in **Guanaboa** and near **Colonel Fuller’s Plantation**.

**Cleavers with fewer leaves and a smooth seed.** <note>original: "Aparine paucioribus foliis semine lævi." Cleavers, or "sticky willy," is known for its seeds and leaves that cling to fur and clothing.</note> I found this in the woods at the roadsides toward **Guanaboa**.

**An anomalous plant with a Cleavers-like leaf and a round seed vessel containing many very small seeds.** <note>original: "Aparines folio anomala..."</note> I once collected this plant in the island of **Barbados** or one of the **Caribbean Islands**.

The largest **Bindweed**, with a stem covered in blunt small spines, a white flower, and an angular ivy-like leaf. It grows most abundantly on the banks of the *Cobre* and *Black Rivers*.

The greater **Bindweed**, seven-leaved with a sulfur-colored, fragrant, and most beautiful flower. *Spanish arbor vine*, or *Spanish woodbind*. It thrives among the trees near the banks of the *Rio Cobre*, not far from the city of *St. Jago de la Vega* <note>Now known as Spanish Town, Jamaica.</note>.

**Bindweed**, five-leaved with a pale yellowish flower and a hairy, stinging stem. American five-leaved **Bindweed**, smooth with rough and thorny tendrils. *The Botanical Paradise of the Batavians, p. 326.* Smooth American five-leaved **Bindweed**. *Plukenet, Table 167, fig. 6.* It is frequently found on the banks of rivers and in meadows.

Smaller five-leaved **Bindweed** with a purple flower. I collected it growing among prickly pears <note>original: "opuntias"</note> in a meadow near the city of *St. Jago de la Vega*.

Greater many-flowered **Bindweed**, creeping very long and very wide with smaller, fragrant white flowers. Many-flowered **Bindweed**, with a roundish leaf and yellow flower. # The Islands of Jamaica, etc.

**Smaller edible Arum, with dark green arrowhead-shaped leaves.** <note>original: "Arum minus esculentum, sagittariæ foliis viridi-nigricantibus."</note> Smaller Arum with arrowhead leaves from the Island of Barbados. *Plukenet’s Phytographia, table 149, figure 2.* Another *Tajaoba* or *mangarapeuna*. *Piso (1648 edition), page 95.* Second *Tajaoba*. *Marcgraf, page 35; Piso (1658 edition), page 236.* **Caribbean Cabbage.** <note>original: "Choux Caraibes." Despite the name, this refers to a type of taro or dasheen whose leaves are eaten like greens.</note> *Du Tertre, page 98.* Perhaps the *Small Arum of Ceylon with arrowhead leaves* from the *Paradisus Batavus*? Or the *Mountain Arum* of *Alpinus’s Exotic Plants, page 335*? Found alongside the previously mentioned species.

**Larger rock-dwelling Arum, with rounder leaves and purple fruit.** <note>original: "Arum saxatile majus, foliis rotundioribus, fructu purpureo."</note> It is found in shady, rocky forests near **Guanaboa** <note>A district in St. Catherine Parish, Jamaica.</note>, as well as on the banks of the river called **Hope River** in **Liguanea** <note>The plain where modern-day Kingston and St. Andrew are located.</note>.

**Arum with a jointed stem and Indian Reed leaves, which renders those who taste the tips of its stalks mute.** <note>original: "Arum caule geniculato, cannæ Indicæ foliis, fummis labris degustantes mutos reddens." This is the infamous "Dumb Cane" (Dieffenbachia).</note> Reeds near the banks of the **Caurwo** river similar to sugar canes, poisonous, and swelling the tongue beyond measure, hindering the ability to speak. *Laet, page 646.* The seventh poisonous tree in the Islands of the Cannibals, etc. *Johnston’s Dendrology, page 467.* Stem-growing Arum with Indian Reed leaves. *Plumier, page 41, figures 61 and 51, letter h.* Perhaps the *Aninga iba* of *Marcgraf, page 106*? Or the second *Aninga* of *Piso, page 220*? **The poisoned Cane of Ligon, page 69. The Dumb Cane.** It is found everywhere in the damper places of the Island of Jamaica. <note>The plant contains calcium oxalate crystals which cause intense swelling and temporary loss of speech if ingested.</note>

**Largest Arum climbing the tallest trees, with jagged water-lily leaves.** <note>original: "Arum maximum altissimas scandens arbores, foliis nympheæ laciniatis."</note> A plant whose leaves serve to wrap the thighs and legs of those suffering from dropsy <note>original: "hydropiques." Dropsy is an old term for edema or swelling caused by fluid retention.</note>. *Du Tertre, page 97?* Sterile and jagged ivy-like Colocasia. *Plumier, page 38, figures 51 and 53.* It occurs frequently in the larger forests of the Caribbean Islands and Jamaica.

**Largest climbing Arum, jointed and three-leaved, with leaves eared at the base.** <note>original: "Arum maximum scandens geniculatum & trifoliatum, foliis ad basin auriculatis."</note> Perhaps the *Hiuca* or *Mizmaitl* of *Hernandez, page 378*? Ivy-like Arum, three-leaved and eared. *Plumier, page 41, figures 58 and 51, letter e.* Found with the former.

**Small, creeping, rock-dwelling Arum, jointed and three-leaved.** <note>original: "Arum saxatile, repens, minus, geniculatum & trifoliatum."</note> Found along the road leading toward the **16 mile walk** <note>A historic route in Jamaica through the Rio Cobre canyon.</note>, in rocky and shady woods.

**Broad-leaved sterile ivy-like Colocasia.** <note>original: "Colocasia hederacea sterilis latifolia."</note> *Plumier, page 37, figure 51, letter a, and figure 52.* Found in the forests of the Island of **Nevis** <note>original: "Nieves."</note>.

**Smaller sterile ivy-like Colocasia with a heart-shaped leaf.** <note>original: "Colocasia hederacea sterilis minor folio cordato."</note> *Plumier, page 39, figure 51, letter d, and figure 55.* It is frequent in the shady forests of the Caribbean Islands and Jamaica.

## *Whorled Herbs.*
<note>original: "Herba Verticillatæ." These are plants whose flowers or leaves grow in whorls—circles around the stem at the same level—typical of the mint family.</note>

**Greater Sage with bluish-grey serrated leaves.** <note>original: "Salvia major folio glauco serrato."</note> I collected this on the Island of **Madeira** near the city of **Funchal**.

**Teucrium-like plant with small pods, laurel-like leaves, and hooded and lipped flowers.** <note>original: "Teucroides filiculosum foliis laurinis, floribus galeatis & labiatis."</note> Found on the Island of **Barbados**.

**Upright shrubby Pennyroyal with very dense whorls.** <note>original: "Pulegium fruticosum erectum verticillis densissimis."</note> **Jamaican Scabious with hyssop-like leaves, or a globular plant with flower heads at the joints and many leaves surrounding them in a star-like whorled pattern.** <note>original: "Scabiosa Jamaicensis hyssopifolia seu globularia capitulis ad genicula foliis plurimis stellatim ambientibus verticillata."</note> Perhaps the *Tzicatzon tecomatl* or *ant's head* of Hernandez. *Plukenet’s Phytographia, table 58, figure 6.* It is very frequent and found everywhere in the meadows around the city of **St. Jago de la Vega** <note>Now known as Spanish Town, Jamaica.</note>.

**Pennyroyal with very long and very broad leaves.** <note>original: "Pulegium longissimis latissimisque foliis."</note> I collected this plant in one of the **Caribbee Islands**.

**Greatest Wild Mint, with a blue flower and the scent of nard.** <note>original: "Mentastrum maximum, flore cæruleo, nardi odore."</note> **Lemon Balm** <note>original Portuguese: "Erva Cidreira."</note> of the Portuguese. *Marcgraf, page 32.* A species of wild **Melissa**. *Piso (1658 edition), page 242.* Perhaps the *Huitxiqua* of Hernandez? Or Ximenez? *Is it the Spikenard, from which a precious oil may be made, mentioned by Wilson in Purchas, book 6, chapter 5, page 1264? Indian Spikenard.* It is abundant in the meadows around the city of **St. Jago de la Vega**, and in the sandy maritime areas near **Old Harbour**.

**Vervain with roundish serrated leaves and a blue flower.** <note>original: "Verbena folio subrotundo serrato flore cæruleo."</note> Two-seeded American Vervain with a skullcap-like leaf, perhaps the Indian Vervain of Bontius. *Plukenet, table 70, figure 1.* Perhaps the Vervain of Monardes? Or the Peruvian Vervain which, according to Monardes as cited by Dalechamps, resembles the Spanish variety. *Bauhin’s Pinax, page 269?* Perhaps the evergreen Peruvian Vervain. *Jean Bauhin, volume 3, book 30, page 444? Chabrée, page 479?* Perhaps the Peruvian Vervain of *Parkinson, page 674?* Perhaps the Indian Vervain of *Bontius, page 150?* Perhaps the American tailed Vervain with pale blue flowers. *Munting, page 542?* **Vervaine.** It grows most abundantly at the edges of roads, in meadows, etc., in **Jamaica** and the **Caribbee Islands**.

**Smallest Vervain with Germander-like leaves.** <note>original: "Verbena minima Chamædryos folio."</note> Found on the banks of the river called **Cobre** <note>The Rio Cobre.</note> below the city of **St. Jago de la Vega**.

**An anomalous plant related to Vervain or Wood Sage, with a whitish flower, a rough calyx, and the smell of garlic.** <note>original: "Verbenæ aut scorodoniæ affinis anomala flore albido, calice aspero, allij odore."</note> **Guiney hen weed.** <note>Guinea Hen Weed (Petiveria alliacea), still known for its strong garlic odor.</note> It grows in shady woods.

**Related to Purslane with a roundish succulent leaf and a five-petaled pale purple flower.** <note>original: "Portulacæ affinis folio subrotundo succulento, flore pentapetalo dilute purpureo."</note> *Horse Purslane*. **Upright shrubby Dogbane with a very large and most beautiful yellow flower.** <note>original: "Apocynum erectum fruticosum flore luteo maximo & speciosissimo."</note> *Savanna Flour*. This most elegant plant flowers in all the lowland meadows of the Island of Jamaica. <term>Apocynum: A genus of plants commonly known as Dogbane, named because some species were historically thought to be poisonous to dogs.</term>

**Smaller Passion Flower with the leaf deeply divided into three non-serrated lobes, and a yellow flower.** <note>original: "Flos passionis minor, folio in tres lacinias non serratas profundiùs diviso, flore luteo."</note> **Passion Flower of Curaçao with a smooth, narrow, three-lobed leaf and the smallest yellowish flower of all, of Hermann,** *Paradise of Batavia*, page 335. **Plukenet,** *Phytographia*, table 210, figure 3. **Larger Indian Clematis with an ivy-like leaf and olive-shaped fruit, of Plumier,** page 70, figure 84. This occurs in the rocky, mountainous fields and gravelly places of the Island of Jamaica.

**Smaller Passion Flower with the leaf divided into three non-serrated, less deep lobes.** <note>original: "Flos passionis minor, folio in tres lacinias non serratas, minus profundas, diviso."</note> **Ivy-like Passion Flower Clematis with a yellow flower, of Munting’s** *Cultivated Plants*, page 422. **Three-leaved Passion Clematis with a yellow flower, of Morison’s** *History of Plants*, part 2, page 7. **The cucumber called the ivy-leaved Passion Flower with a yellowish-green flower, of Hermann’s** *Catalog of Plants*, page 205. **Another creeping Indian Balsam with the leaves of tree-ivy and a greenish flower, of Ambrosinus’s** *Phytologia*, page 91.

**Dandelion with the leaf hoary underneath and a purple flower.** <note>original: "Dens leonis, folio subtus incano, flore purpureo."</note> **Yztac cihuatlis, or "white woman."** <note>This name comes from Nahuatl, the language of the Aztecs, recorded by Spanish naturalists.</note> Hernandez. **Yztaccihvatl.** Ximenez. *I collected this in the fields of Mr. Cope, in the place called Guanaboa.*

**Greater scentless fleabane with an entire, dry, and hard elecampane-leaf, and a white chicory-like flower emerging from the sides of the branches.** <note>original: "Conyza major inodora, helenij folio integro sicco & duro, cichorij flore albo è ramorum lateribus exeunte."</note> *It grows abundantly with the preceding species, as well as near the river called Cobre, and in the meadow called Moneque Savanna.*

**Scentless fleabane with an entire, hard, narrow, and oblong elecampane-leaf, with the flower heads clustered on the sides of the branches.** <note>original: "Conyza inodora, helenij folio, integro, duro, angusto, oblongo, capitulis in lateribus ramorum conglomeratis."</note> *It is frequent and easily found on the mountain called Diablo.*

**Shrubby fleabane with the scent of rock-rose, with pale purple flowers sitting at the tips of the small branches, and smaller heads and seeds.** <note>original: "Conyza fruticosa, cisti odore, floribus pallide purpureis, summitatibus ramulorum insidentibus, capitulis & semine minoribus."</note> *It is found along the road that leads from the city of St. Jago de la Vega toward Guanaboa, and in sunnier places on Mount Diablo.*

# Catalog of Plants

**Shrubby fleabane with the scent of rockrose, with pale purple flowers sitting at the ends of the branches, and with larger flower heads and seeds.** <note>original: "Conyza fruticosa cisti odore, floribus pallide purpureis summitatibus ramulorum insidentibus, capitulis & semine majoribus."</note> Found with the previous plant.

**Shrubby fleabane with a spear-shaped leaf and a pale purple flower.** <note>original: "Conyza fruticosa, folio hastato, flore pallide purpureo."</note> This is the **American hemp-like fleabane with soft, gray leaves and large heads** <note>original: "Eupatoria conyzoides folio molli & incano capitulis magnis Americana."</note> in Plukenet's *Phytographia*, plate 177, figure 3. Perhaps it is the **Thin Axixpatlis** or **five-sided twining plant** <note>original: "Axixpatlis Texaxahuacensis seu volubilis quinquelatera."</note> mentioned by Hernandez? <note>Francisco Hernandez was a 16th-century physician who documented Mexican flora; "Axixpatlis" is a Nahuatl name.</note> It grows in all the meadows and hills of the Island of Jamaica.

**Shrubby fleabane with a pale purple flower, with flower heads emerging in spikes from the sides of the branches.** <note>original: "Conyza fruticosa flore pallide purpureo, capitulis è lateribus ramulorum spicatim exeuntibus."</note> Called ***Tremate*** by the Brazilians in Marcgraf, pages 61 and 81, and ***Tremae*** in Piso (1658 edition), page 176. It grows in the thickets and more open woods of Jamaica and the Caribbean Islands.

**Larger scented fleabane or baccharis, with naked purple flowers.** <note>original: "Conyza major odorata seu baccharis, floribus purpureis nudis."</note> I found it in maritime marshes near the house of Mr. Delacree, in the place called **Liguanea**. <note>Liguanea is the plain where modern-day Kingston, Jamaica, is located.</note>

**Fleabane with nettle-like leaves.** <note>original: "Conyza urticae folio."</note> I collected this in Jamaica and the Caribbean Islands.

**Fleabane with a spear-shaped or triangular, serrated, smooth leaf.** <note>original: "Conyza folio hastato seu triangulari serrato glabro."</note> It grows in the place called **16 mile walk** in the fields of Mr. Nedham. <note>The "Sixteen Mile Walk" was a historic district in the parish of St. Thomas-in-the-Vale, Jamaica.</note>

**Smaller, low-lying, stinking fleabane with a yellow flower and seeds covered in down.** <note>original: "Conyza minor procumbens foetida, flore luteo, seminibus tomento obductis."</note> It is found everywhere in the sunnier wooded areas of the Island of Jamaica.

**Aster with an oblong, entire, gray-haired leaf and a pale blue flower.** <note>original: "Aster folio oblongo integro incano flore pallide coeruleo."</note> I observed this in the wetter parts of the meadows around the town of *St. Jago de la Vega*. <note>St. Jago de la Vega is the historic Spanish Town, the former capital of Jamaica.</note>

**Undescribed annual Canadian aster.** <note>original: "Aster Canadensis annuus non descriptus."</note> Cited in Brunyer’s *Catalog of the Blois Garden*, page 10. **Annual Canadian aster with downy flowers.** <note>original: "Aster Canadensis annuus flore papposo."</note> From the *Catalog of the Royal Garden of Paris*, page 27. **Hairy annual Virginian goldenrod with a pale flower.** <note>original: "Virga aurea Virginiana irsuta annua di fiore pallido."</note> From Zannoni, page 204. **Sharp, white Canadian groundsel.** <note>original: "Senecio Canadensis acris alba."</note> From Morison’s *Blois Garden*, page 190. **Sharp, white annual fleabane.** <note>original: "Conyza acris annua alba."</note> Also from Morison, page 256. **Sharp, white, annual Canadian fleabane with a toadflax leaf.** <note>original: "Conyza Canadensis annua acris alba linariae folio."</note> From Boccone’s *Sicilian Plants*, page 85. Ray’s *History*, page 271. **Narrow-leaved American hemp-agrimony.** <note>original: "Eupatorium Cannabinum Americanum angusti-folium."</note> Parkinson, page 595. It grows everywhere in Jamaica and the Caribbean islands.

**Taller "Alypum" or "Terrible Herb," with ash-colored rough bark and a longer pointed leaf.** <note>original: "Alypum sive Herba terribilis procerior, cortice cinereo scabro, folio acuminato longiore." Alypum, or Globularia, was known as the "Terrible Herb" due to its powerful and potentially dangerous purgative effects.</note> I collected this near the city of **Funchal** on the island of **Madeira**.

**Larger groundsel with a purple flower-cup.** <note>original: "Senecio major florum calice purpureo."</note> I observed this growing in the fields of Mr. Nedham, especially those under cultivation, in the place called **16 mile walk**.

### Island of Jamaica, etc.

**Smaller groundsel with the leaf of the larger ox-eye daisy.** <note>original: "Senecio minor bellidis majoris folio."</note> This grows on the banks of the river called Cobre, near the city of **St. Jago de la Vega**. <note>Now known as Spanish Town, the former capital of Jamaica.</note>

**Larger goldenrod, or Doria’s herb, with a wavy, hairy leaf.** <note>original: "Virga aurea major sive herba Doria folio sinuato hirsuto."</note> It grows along the road that leads from the fields of **Mr. Cope** toward **Mountain River**.

**Everlasting flower with a winged stem and flowers in spikes.** <note>original: "Helichrysum caule alato, floribus spicatis."</note> It occurs abundantly in the drier meadows of the Island of Jamaica.

**The second everlasting flower, or one similar to the wild everlasting with an oblong flower.** <note>original: "Helichrysum 2um seu Helichryso Sylvestri flore oblongo similis."</note> Referenced in Bauhin’s *Pinax*, page 265 and *Prodromus*, page 123. It is related to the **other scented yellow cassidony of Lobelius** <note>original: "Stæchadi citrinæ alteri odoræ Lobelij affinis"</note> but with shorter heads, as noted in Jean Bauhin, volume 3, book 26, page 157; Ray, page 282; and the **wilder yellow cassidony** in Parkinson, page 688. I collected this near the city of **Funchal** on the island of **Madeira**.

**Cudweed approaching the yellow cassidony.** <note>original: "Gnaphalium ad Stæchadem citrinam accedens."</note> Citations include Jean Bauhin, volume 3, book 26, page 160; Ray’s *History*, page 284; and Chabrey, page 371. Perhaps it is the **eighth or wild broad-leaved everlasting with clustered heads** <note>original: "Helichrysum 8um seu Sylvestre latifolium capitulis conglobatis"</note> in Bauhin’s *Pinax*, page 264? Or the **wild everlasting** in Gerard’s *Emaculatus*, page 647? Or the **gold-locks and wild everlasting** of Lobelius’s *Icons*, page 485? Or perhaps **Plateau’s second cudweed** in Clusius’s *History of Rare Plants*, page 263? Or the **ninth or larger cudweed with a broad oblong leaf** in Bauhin’s *Pinax*, page 263? See also Plukenet, table 31, figure 6; the **low-lying cudweed with an oblong leaf** in Parkinson, page 686; Gerard’s *Emaculatus*, page 643; and Ray’s *History*, page 296. It is found with the previous plant, where it varies wonderfully in its height, the narrowness and length of its leaves, its frequency, and the elegance of its flower heads.

**Shrubby maritime ox-eye daisy, with bluish-gray oblong leaves and a yellow flower.** <note>original: "Chrysanthemum fruticosum maritimum, foliis glaucis oblongis, flore luteo."</note> Identified as the **ox-eye daisy from the Caribbean Islands with hoary, silky, silver, and thick stock-like leaves** <note>original: "Chrysanthemum ex Insulis Charibæis leucoii incanis & sericeis foliis argenteis crassis"</note> in Plukenet, table 115, figure 4. I observed this growing on the rocky sea shore near the city of the Island of Jamaica formerly called **Sevilla** by the Spaniards. <note>Sevilla la Nueva, the first Spanish capital of Jamaica, near modern St. Ann's Bay.</note>

**Ox-eye daisy with a wrinkled, rough, oblong sage-like leaf.** <note>original: "Chrysanthemum Salviæ folio rugoso scabro oblongo."</note> I collected this plant in **Jamaica** or one of the **Caribbean** islands and placed it among my dried specimens, but I do not remember which one. <note>A rare admission of a lapse in the collector's records.</note>

**Climbing three-leaved ox-eye daisy with a yellow flower and a long, beaked, two-toothed seed.** <note>original: "Chrysanthemum trifoliatum scandens, flore luteo, semine longo rostrato bidente."</note> Perhaps the **American ox-eye daisy with a smooth chickpea leaf and a large daisy flower** <note>original: "Chrysanthemum Americanum ciceris folio glabro, flore bellidis majoris"</note> in Hermann’s *Paradisus Batavus*, page 323? It is found in the inland forests of the Island of Jamaica, where sometimes the leaves are winged.

# Of the Island of Jamaica, etc.

...plants sent from the Island of Bermuda to the most diligent botanist Mr. James Pettiver; I observed this one among them.

**The plant from which moxa is gathered, perhaps common mugwort.** <note>original: "Planta de qua moxa colligitur, forte artemisia vulgaris." Moxa is a soft, downy substance burned on the skin in traditional medicine, a practice Hans Sloane would have encountered in accounts of Eastern medicine.</note> Jean Bauhin, volume 3, book 26, page 184. Whether this is the **Chinese mugwort whose soft down is called moxa**, <note>original: "Artemisia Chinensis cujus mollugo moxa dicitur."</note> perhaps the **Ytzecuinpatli** of Mexico <note>A Nahuatl name meaning "dog-medicine herb."</note> mentioned by Hernandez, or the **Virginian mugwort** mentioned by Parkinson and Plukenet (table 15, figure 1)? On the island of Barbados, I obtained a plant from the garden of a man very inquisitive in natural matters, who was cultivating it as the "moxa plant"; he reported that he had received it from the East Indies. Upon comparing a specimen shared with me against the common mugwort, I found it scarcely differed from it.

**Lower mugwort with a larger white flower, similar to the feverfew called Achoavan, with hedge-mustard leaves and the taste of wormwood, from Jamaica.** <note>original: "Artemisia humilior flore majore albo. Matricariæ Achoavan dictæ similis, erisymi foliis, absinthij sapore Jamaicensis." Plukenet, table 45, figure 3.</note> ***Wild Wormwood***. It grows everywhere in gravelly places in the open meadows around the city called **St. Jago de la Vega**. <note>Now known as Spanish Town, Jamaica.</note>

**A forest anomaly related to the Scabious, with elecampane-like leaves, individual white florets in the same head having their own protective leaves, and a downy seed.** <note>original: "Scabiosæ affinis anomala sylvatica, enulæ folio, singulis flosculis albis in eodem capitulo perianthia habentibus, femine papposo." This refers to a member of the daisy family (Asteraceae) with seeds designed to be carried by the wind.</note> This is found in the woods along the road leading from the city of **St. Jago de la Vega** toward the fields of Mr. **Cope** in **Guanaboa**, and in other inland forests of the Island of Jamaica.

**Stinking Eryngo with narrow, serrated leaves.** <note>original: "Eryngium foliis angustis serratis fætidum." This plant is *Eryngium foetidum*, commonly known today as Culantro or Spiritweed, used widely in Caribbean cooking and medicine.</note> The **Stinking American Eryngo** called **Itubu** by the people of Suriname. <note>Hermann, *Catalogus Plantarum*, page 236.</note> The **Cohayelli** or **Chichicahoazton**, or "herb with serrated leaves" described by Hernandez on page 143. Ximenez describes it as "a herb that has leaves serrated in the manner of a comb." <note>original Spanish: "que es yerva que tiene las ojas aserradas à manera de peyne."</note> It abounds in the damp and richer fields around the house of Mr. **Bourden** and the place called **the Crescent Plantation**.

<header>The Island of Jamaica, etc.</header>

...[cirma?]. <note>original: "cirma"</note> **Nieremberg**, page 295? Wood imitating the color of boxwood. <note>original: "Lignum buxi colorem imitans." Boxwood is known for its fine grain and yellow color.</note> **Léry**, part 3, West Indies, page 297? **De Laet**, page 562? **Bouix**. **Linschoten?** American wood of a boxwood color. **Jean Bauhin**, volume 1, page 498? **Chabrée**, appendix page 598? Whether this is the *Holly of Laudonnière, page 3?* *Hakluyt, part 3, page 305?* Or the *Holm Trees* of **Alvaro Nuñez** in *Purchas, book 8, chapter 1, page 1502?* I observed it growing in a maritime forest at the place called **Don Christopher's Cove**, near the ruins of the city formerly called **Sevilla** by the Spaniards <note>Sevilla la Nueva, the first Spanish capital of Jamaica</note>.

A berry-bearing shrub with flowers like a Turnsole <term>Heliotropium: plants named for turning toward the sun</term>, growing in clusters, with a wrinkled, foul-smelling, very large roundish hairy leaf, and white fruit. It grows abundantly in the more open places of the Island of Jamaica near the house of Sir **Watson** <note>original: "Dom. Watson eq. aurat." (Knight Bachelor)</note> in the place called **the seven Plantations**.

A shrub with flowers like a Turnsole, with a very large, oblong, pointed, and smooth leaf. Found with the previous one.

A Bramble <note>original: "Rubus"</note> with longer leaves covered underneath with a soft down and gray-white, with smaller flowers and fruit. *Blackberries of the Island of Hispaniola* <note>original Spanish: "Carcamoras de la Ysla Espannola"</note> *by Oviedo. Creeping brambles nourishing mulberries* <note>original Latin: "Serpentia rubeta mororum altricia"</note> *by Peter Martyr, decade 3, chapter 8.* I collected this along the road that goes toward **St. Ann’s**, in the place called **the Moneque Savanna** <note>modern Moneague</note>.

A berry-bearing shrub with an oblong, smooth-edged leaf, and a five-petaled, pale yellow, very fragrant flower. *Cloven Berries*. I observed this in the wooded hills called **red hills**, and also in the place called **Caymanes**.

A berry-bearing shrub with a five-petaled blue flower and violet fruit. I found it in the rocky hills near the house of Mr. **Batchelor**.

**A climbing shrubby plant** whose stem is used in place of a string for musical instruments. **A shrubby yellow root**, similar to liquorice <note>original: "glycyrrhizæ similis"</note>, with dark bark, used for cleaning the teeth. This root is kept for the aforementioned use by the Black people, who dig it out from the more open woods of the Island of Jamaica.
